name: Zechariah
role: Prophet of the return, whose visions filled the night
whenBasis: His dated oracles run from the second to the fourth year of Darius I (Zechariah 1:1, 7:1).
summary: Son of Berechiah, son of Iddo, a prophet who with Haggai encouraged the rebuilding of the temple. In one night he saw eight visions: a rider among the myrtles, horns and craftsmen, a man with a measuring line, the high priest Joshua reclothed, a lampstand between two olive trees, a flying scroll, a woman in a basket, and four chariots. His book goes on to the king coming to Zion on a donkey, thirty pieces of silver, and the one they have pierced, which the gospels read of Jesus.
body: Asked whether to keep the fasts for the fall of Jerusalem, he answers with the LORD's call to justice and mercy, and with a picture of Jerusalem restored: old men and women sitting in its streets, and boys and girls playing there.
Ezra calls him son of Iddo, perhaps the priest of that name who returned with Zerubbabel.

later.text: Chapters 9–14 have no dates, visions or named figures of the return, and Carol and Eric Meyers assign them to a later hand (Second Zechariah). C. F. Keil holds that the differences do not point to two or three prophets, and that the people after the exile are the setting of these chapters too.

later.text: Jesus speaks of Zechariah son of Berechiah, murdered between the sanctuary and the altar. This prophet is the son of Berechiah, but no account of his death survives; 2 Chronicles tells of the priest Zechariah son of Jehoiada, stoned in the temple court. The Targum of Lamentations has “Zechariah son of Iddo, the High Priest and faithful prophet” killed in the temple on the Day of Atonement. Heinrich Meyer and E. H. Plumptre take Jesus to mean Jehoiada's son, and the name Berechiah to be an error: of oral tradition, for Meyer; of a copyist, for Plumptre. Meyer reports Hammond, Hug and others reading it of the Zechariah son of Baruch whom, Josephus says, the Zealots killed in the temple.
